transcript:
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
With less than six weeks to go before the midterm elections, registered voters say by
12-point margin that they'd prefer to elect a Democrat to Congress over a Republican.
That's one of the findings of the new NPR/PBS News mayor's poll.
The survey finds more voters believe Democrats would do a better job than Republicans in addressing
high gas prices and the economy in general.
There is growing concern that President Trump could deploy federalized National Guard troops
around polling locations in the upcoming election.
That's despite clear laws barring such action.
Here's NPR's Kat Lonsdorf.
A growing number of Democratic lawmakers, retired military leaders, and civil society
organizations are seeking assurance from the Trump administration that the military will
not be deployed to polling places, while also preparing for such a move to occur.
Performing federal troops or armed agents near the polls is clearly barred by federal law.
But President Trump and several other key officials have recently sidestepped direct
lines of questioning around the issue.
And Trump has already shown a willingness to deploy the military domestically, particularly
the National Guard.
Meanwhile, voting officials across the country say they plan on administering the midterms
as usual and are assuring voters there are plans in place if federal agents do show up
to the polls.
Kat Lonsdorf, NPR News.
The day after President Trump stood before the U.N. General Assembly and threatened to
annihilate Iran if it did not agree to a deal.
This morning, the president of Iran told the international gathering in New York his country
is the victim of U.S. and Israeli aggression.
And Pierre's Hadil Al-Shalchi with the latest.
In his speech to the U.N. General Assembly, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshqian said that
Iran's defensive systems were built to defend his country, so that "no one can think that
bombing Iranian cities will go unanswered."
He held up a picture of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and Iranian schoolgirls who were killed in
U.S.-Israeli strikes in February and called the U.S., quote, "terrorists," prompting
the one U.S. representative in the assembly hall to walk out.
Pezeshqian denied that Iran wanted a nuclear weapon and refused limitations on its civilian
nuclear program.
On Tuesday, Iranian and U.S. delegations met via mediators for three hours, according to
President Trump.
President Trump said Iran must decide whether it will agree to a deal or face, quote, "obliteration."
Hadil Al-Shalchi, NPR News, Istanbul.
The United States and China are preparing for a high-stakes meeting in Washington, D.C.,
starting tonight.
President Trump is hosting Chinese leader Xi Jinping on his first state visit to the United
States in more than a decade.
The leaders of the world's two biggest economies are attempting to avoid another trade war.
However, the relationship remains fragile in light of their respective geopolitical interests
and rivalry in advanced technologies, including A.I.
This is NPR News.
As leading tech executives call for a pause in A.I. development, smaller A.I. labs are
pushing back.
NPR's Bobby Allen reports a fear is that an A.I. slowdown will lock in the dominance of
the bigger players.
Anthropic stereo Amade, open A.I. Sam Altman, SpaceX A.I., Zilon Musk cannot agree on much.
But they all favor pacing A.I. development, with fears mounting about artificial intelligence
escaping human control.
Some of the loudest critics have been middle-of-the-pack A.I. companies like Proplexity, Cohere, and
Mistral.
In statements to NPR, those companies say a slowdown now would cement the advantages of
the biggest labs.
Some even say small A.I. companies might be forced to shut down.
The slowdown calls come as Anthropic and open A.I. race towards initial public offerings,
as each company's rampant spending on computing power puts pressure on their balance sheets.
We should note, Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR.
Bobby Allen, NPR News.
In New York, former production assistant Mimi Haley is praising a judge's decision to sentence
ex-movie producer Harvey Weinstein to 15 years in prison for sexually assaulting her in 2006.
She described the toll on her from a years-long legal battle that resulted in Weinstein's
retrial.
It was a really tough thing to do, I have to say, and I thought of not doing it many
times.
I thought of pulling out.
Weinstein is also awaiting resentencing on a separate rape case in California he pleaded
not guilty to all charges.
A Food and Drug Administration advisory panel is weighing whether to recommend approval
of a new blood test for early detection of various forms of cancer in people 50 and older,
oncologists are divided on whether Grail, Inc.'s technology is ready to go public.
This is NPR.

Democratic lawmakers and military leaders seek assurance Trump won't deploy troops at polling places
Iranian President Pezeshqian tells UN his country is victim of U.S. and Israeli aggression
President Trump hosts Chinese leader Xi Jinping for first state visit in over a decade
Smaller AI labs push back against calls for development pause by tech executives
Former production assistant Mimi Haley praises judge's sentence of Harvey Weinstein to 15 years
FDA advisory panel considers approval of Grail Inc.'s blood test for early cancer detection
